Act I · Setup

Easy to set up.

Bring the AI assistant you already use, say what you want to learn, put it in order, and you can start.

  • 01 Bring your agent

    Claude Code, Codex or Claude Desktop, on your own subscription or API key.

  • 02 Say what you want to learn

    One sentence like “I want to learn how levers work,” or a YAML or Markdown outline.

  • 03 Arrange the course

    The concept map, what comes each day and when to review are laid out for you. Change them until they’re right, then generate.

Act II · Learn

One window.

Slides, whiteboard, notes and the AI tutor on one screen, with no switching back and forth.

  1. Read the same lesson as slides, an article or a transcript. Arrange the whiteboard, notes and tutor on one screen the way you like.

  2. Highlights stay on the text and notes stay pinned to their page, right where you left them.

  3. Stuck? Ask on the page you’re on. Summaries and examples come without switching windows.

  4. If it won’t click, draw it. Sketches and working are saved with the lesson.

  5. Search notes, highlights and conversations together, then see on the learning map what each lesson left behind.

  6. Pack handouts, notes and the learning map together, as files on your own computer.

Act III · Review

Methodologically open.

When to review and what comes next aren’t guesses. Every method says where it comes from.

  • Corbett & Anderson

    Knowledge tracing: Modeling the acquisition of procedural knowledge

    Every answer updates how likely you are to know each concept.

    1995

  • Roediger & Karpicke

    Test-enhanced learning: Taking memory tests improves long-term retention

    Short quizzes through the lesson: recalling instead of rereading.

    2006

  • Black & Wiliam

    Assessment and classroom learning

    Quizzes are frequent and low-stakes, and the explanation shows right after you answer.

    1998

  • Ebbinghaus

    Memory: A contribution to experimental psychology

    Without review we forget, so a review should come just before you would.

    1885

  • Cepeda, Pashler, Vul, Wixted & Rohrer

    Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis

    Intervals stretch from an hour to 14 days, scheduled from your answers.

    2006

  • Anderson & Krathwohl

    A taxonomy for learning, teaching, and assessing

    Questions aim at understanding, applying and analysing, not just recall.

    2001

The papers and the implementation notes are in the source code.

Take it with you

Export it in one pack.

  • Course handouts (PDF)
  • Session notes: highlights, whiteboard images, conversations
  • Learning map
  • Mind map
  • References

The files stay on your own computer.
